stem.text: What is a reason for a central bank to decrease the interest rate?

options.text: to attract hot money inflows to prevent a decrease in the exchange rate
to discourage private sector borrowing for investment
to increase aggregate demand and aggregate supply in the economy
to slow the rate of increase of domestic prices

explanation.text: A lower interest rate reduces the cost of borrowing and the return on saving, encouraging both households to spend more (consumption) and firms to borrow and invest more — both components of aggregate demand. The resulting higher investment also expands the economy's productive capacity over time, which can raise aggregate supply.

optionAnalysis.text: A lower interest rate makes a country's assets less attractive to foreign investors, causing hot money outflows (not inflows) and a likely depreciation (not prevention of a decrease) in the exchange rate.
A lower interest rate encourages, not discourages, private sector borrowing for investment, since borrowing becomes cheaper.
Lower interest rates stimulate both consumption and investment spending (raising aggregate demand) and, through higher investment, can expand productive capacity (raising aggregate supply) over time.
A lower interest rate is expansionary and tends to increase, not slow, demand-pull inflationary pressure on domestic prices — raising interest rates is the usual tool to slow inflation.

reasoningChain: Recall that a lower interest rate reduces the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving.
This encourages higher consumption (cheaper borrowing, less incentive to save) and higher investment (cheaper to finance), both raising aggregate demand.
Higher investment can also expand the economy's capital stock and productive capacity, raising aggregate supply.
Rule out the other options, which describe effects that actually follow from raising, not lowering, interest rates (attracting hot money, discouraging borrowing, slowing inflation).

inferredMistakes.text: Confusing the effects of lowering interest rates with the effects of raising them — e.g. assuming a rate cut attracts hot money or slows inflation, when both of those are effects of a rate increase instead.
